title: Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. (Aug 2004 TCC) Tax Court Case
subject: Seafood processor SR&ED appeal concerning whether crab processing and preservation methods qualified as SR&ED.
summary: Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. The Queen, 2004 TCC 553, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian claimants under the Income Tax Act. The Court held that commercial fishery development was not SR&ED, that only materials used up or rendered valueless qualify as materials consumed, and that renovations to leased premises used solely for SR&ED can qualify.
metaDescription: Explore the August 2004 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit qualification.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Blue Wave Seafoods Incorporated and D'Eon Fisheries Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2004 TCC 553 (subsequently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. Canada, 2006 FCA 81), stands as a foundational authority in Canadian tax jurisprudence governing the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program. Adjudicated under the General Procedure by Justice Campbell J. Miller on August 11, 2004, the ruling delineates the statutory boundaries between commercial industry pioneering and eligible scientific or technological investigation under the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act") and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C. 1978, c. 945 (the "Regulations"). Furthermore, the judgment provides critical judicial interpretation regarding the eligibility of bulk raw materials under the proxy method of expenditure calculation and the deductibility of capital renovations to leased premises dedicated to SR&ED prosecution.
Factual and Operational Context

The Appellants, D'Eon Fisheries Limited ("D'Eon") and Blue Wave Seafoods Incorporated ("Blue Wave"), were connected corporate entities operating in Nova Scotia under the presidency of Mr. Sylvain D'Eon, with Mr. Nelson Burbidge, a chartered accountant, serving as minority shareholder, director, and secretary-treasurer hired in 1990 to manage developmental costs. Throughout the 1990s, the Appellants endeavoured to establish and commercialize a domestic Canadian fishery for silver hake (Merluccius bilinearis). Historically regarded by the domestic commercial fishing sector as a "trash fish," silver hake is a small, delicate, white-fleshed groundfish whose skeletal structure makes manual processing exceptionally difficult and whose flesh deteriorates rapidly after harvest. During the late 1980s, silver hake was harvested 50 to 125 miles offshore on the Scotian Shelf using small-mesh gear exclusively by foreign fleets—predominantly Russian and Cuban—which froze the fish at sea, consistent with the belief of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) that the species could not be landed fresh but had to be frozen at sea. Seeking to diversify Atlantic fisheries, the Government of Canada designated silver hake as one of 21 underutilized species and solicited industry proposals to develop a domestic Canadian silver hake fishery.

The Appellants' operational efforts evolved through several distinct chronological phases, beginning with initial foreign fleet ventures and early processing trials between 1990 and 1992. In 1990, the Appellants entered into a harvesting arrangement with a Norwegian fleet, which failed due to inappropriate fishing gear. In 1991, the Appellants contracted with Cuban vessels under terms requiring 10% to 15% of the catch to be landed frozen in Canada, where the Appellants thawed, headed, gutted, repacked, and shipped the fish using adapted machinery at a leased processing plant. Concurrently, an exploratory inshore catch conducted between August 21 and September 24, 1991, supplied fresh silver hake for onshore processing trials. An October 1992 DFO technical report evaluating these 1991 trials concluded that storing fish in large insulated containers (Xactic boxes) filled with "slush ice"—a mixture of flaked freshwater ice and a lesser volume of seawater—was superior to boxed ice storage, and identified minced fish flesh as the most viable processing option. However, the resulting mince was poorly received by the Appellants' primary customer, National Sea Products, was never sold at a profit, and could not be diverted into fish meal due to regulatory prohibitions.

A second operational phase centred on Canadianization and specialized machinery adaptation between 1994 and 1996. In 1994, the "Silver Hake Canadianization Committee" was formed by government and industry representatives, including the Appellants, which, according to a study by Coopers & Lybrand Consulting, had a mandate in 1995 to Canadianize and eventually commercialize the silver hake fishing industry in Nova Scotia (the related January 1995 funding proposal was never implemented). After their mince was poorly received, the Appellants worked in conjunction with the Japanese in building equipment to remove water from the fish and, with the technical assistance of a Mr. Shimako, acquired machines from Japan, including a silent cutter and a moulder, the process also requiring dehydrators and freezers. This equipment was configured to manufacture surimi (a refined, dewatered fish protein gel used to fabricate fish balls and fish cakes) and tempura—products never previously produced from silver hake.

The final phase involved inshore fresh fish procurement and a commercial pivot toward whole round marketing between 1995 and 1998. By 1995, Mr. D'Eon recognized that producing top-grade surimi and achieving commercial viability required fresh rather than frozen-at-sea silver hake, necessitating a domestic inshore fishery. Because prevailing market prices of $0.08 per pound were insufficient to incentivize Canadian fishers to target silver hake, Mr. D'Eon offered $0.15 per pound to domestic operators. Two fishing entities accepted this price and harvested silver hake in the LaHave and Emerald basins under exploratory conditions attached to their commercial groundfish licences. Separator grates were used in the gear to reduce by-catch, and, to preserve catch quality at sea, onboard handling evolved from pans in the hold alternating fish and ice (which squashed the fish), to a system of shelves, and finally to tote bags or pans (measuring roughly 3 feet by 1.5 feet) holding 100 pounds of fish in a slushy ice-water mixture—a handling technique Mr. D'Eon testified someone had simply suggested to him, although no one was identified as the source and no time was identified for the suggestion. Because the Appellants maintained that they had no choice but to take the entire catch at $0.15 per pound (although the Court noted there was little evidence of the actual arrangement with the fishers in 1995 and 1996, and no fishers testified), and their leased plant lacked the capacity to process all landed fish into surimi or mince, excess fish was frozen for inventory or sold in a different form, at a loss. By 1997, the Appellants were effectively out of surimi and tempura (only limited production of those products took place thereafter, although mince continued to be produced in both 1997 and 1998), and in 1997 and 1998 most of their efforts went to sorting, icing, packaging, and marketing whole round fresh silver hake.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Minister's Challenge

Having previously filed seven retroactive SR&ED claims for the 1991 to 1994 taxation years in response to a Government-set September 1994 deadline for past SR&ED claims, the Appellants submitted eight SR&ED claims across the 1995, 1996, 1997, and 1998 taxation years, representing one claim per corporation for each year. The 1997 and 1998 claims were filed solely on the basis of a broad project described as the "development of the silver hake fishery," echoing the objective identified in the T661 technical description of their earlier 1991 to 1994 claims, namely "to develop the fishery by first creating methods to harvest the fish, and secondly developing methods to process the fish commercially".

D'Eon's 1995 and 1996 claims were accepted by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) without review, the science and financial reviewers never becoming involved with those two claims. The remaining six claims—Blue Wave's claims for 1995 through 1998, and D'Eon's claims for 1997 and 1998—were the subject of the appeals and were reviewed through CRA's two-stream (science and financial) process, involving Science Advisor Mr. Brian Neil (for the 1996, 1997, and 1998 claims) and Financial Auditor Mr. Bruce Harnish (for the 1995, 1997, and 1998 claims). In the 1995 and 1996 assessments for Blue Wave, the Minister of National Revenue rejected the broad characterization of "developing a Canadian silver hake industry" as eligible SR&ED, but accepted that Blue Wave carried out a qualifying SR&ED sub-project in 1995 and 1996 specifically restricted to developing processing methods for surimi and tempura. However, the Minister allowed only a fraction of the claimed expenditures: Blue Wave's total current expenses of $147,283 as filed for its fiscal year ended July 31, 1995 were reduced to $34,740 on review, and $545,987 as filed for its fiscal year ended July 31, 1996 was reduced to $60,286. Specifically, the CRA disallowed the cost of third-party fresh fish purchased at $0.15 per pound that exceeded surimi trial capacity and was sold commercially or inventoried, and disallowed $27,914 in 1995 contractor costs, which comprised $19,708 for leased plant renovations to accommodate surimi production and $8,206 for plant equipment including fire extinguishers, tables, and trays. For the 1997 and 1998 taxation years, Mr. Neil evaluated both the surimi project and the broader inshore silver hake fishery project for Blue Wave and D'Eon, concluding that neither constituted SR&ED in those years. Consequently, the Minister denied all claimed SR&ED deductions and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) for 1997 and 1998.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The appeals were adjudicated under the interconnected SR&ED provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. At the core of the statutory regime is subsection 248(1) of the Act, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or technological advancement. Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), section 38, and section 127 of the Act govern the pooling and deductibility of current SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada and the qualification of those expenditures for ITCs. Because the Appellants elected under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act (the proxy method), eligible outlays were limited to the categories enumerated in that clause, notably the cost of "materials consumed in the prosecution of scientific research and experimental development" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V); the Court stressed that this election precluded the operation of clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), so that paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations—which treats as directly attributable expenditures that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED and would not have been incurred had it not occurred, for purposes of clause 37(8)(a)(i)(B) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)—did not apply directly and was considered only as interpretive guidance at the Appellants' suggestion. Additionally, subparagraph 37(8)(d)(i) of the Act excludes from SR&ED qualification any capital expenditure made in respect of the acquisition of a building or a leasehold interest in a building.

To operationalize the statutory definition in subsection 248(1), Justice Miller applied the five-criteria analytical framework set out by Associate Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (T.C.C.), which expanded the traditional three-pronged analysis. This framework requires the Court to determine whether there was a technical risk or scientific uncertainty; whether the taxpayer formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty through observation, clear objective setting, articulation of uncertainty, hypothesis formulation, and methodical testing; whether the procedures accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method; whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and whether a detailed record was kept of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Miller dismissed Blue Wave's appeals for the 1996, 1997, and 1998 taxation years and D'Eon's appeals for the 1997 and 1998 taxation years (D'Eon's 1995 and 1996 claims having been accepted without review), and allowed Blue Wave's appeal for the 1995 taxation year only to the extent of referring the matter back to the Minister for reassessment on the basis that $19,708 is a qualified expenditure on SR&ED, awarding costs to the Respondent (the Crown). With respect to 1997 and 1998 eligibility, the Court held that no SR&ED was conducted by either Appellant. By 1997, the Appellants were effectively out of surimi and tempura production and knew how best to catch silver hake to reduce by-catch (e.g., separator grates), how best to keep it on board to maintain freshness (e.g., totes), and that the total allowable catch (TAC) was relatively stable; they knew they could get fresh silver hake to the plant and what to do with it once there. Although the Court found that the onshore handling of whole round fresh fish presented a technological uncertainty, nothing in the nature of hypothesis testing occurred—the fish were simply dumped onto stainless steel tables, sorted, iced, packaged, and shipped; and although the Court characterized the question of fish stock abundance in the LaHave and Emerald basins as a scientific (rather than merely business) uncertainty, it held that the problem was resolvable by standard or routine procedures, so that no scientific uncertainty faced the Appellants in that regard.

Regarding the 1995 and 1996 excess fish expenditures, the Court upheld the Minister's disallowance of third-party fish purchases beyond the quantities directly processed into surimi and tempura. Excess fish sold commercially or frozen in inventory retained monetary value and were neither "consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) nor directly related to SR&ED under Regulation 2900(2)(c), notwithstanding the Appellants' position that they had to buy the entire catch at $0.15 per pound and sold the excess at a loss (Regulation 2900(2)(c) being considered only as interpretive guidance, since it did not apply directly given the election under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). Finally, regarding the 1995 contractor and renovation expenditures, while affirming the disallowance of $8,206 for general equipment (fire extinguishers, tables, and trays), as there was no testimony as to whether that amount pertained to the surimi/tempura production process, Justice Miller overturned the Minister's disallowance of $19,708 expended to renovate the leased processing plant for surimi production. The Court ruled that subparagraph 37(8)(d)(i) bars only the capital cost of acquiring a building or a leasehold interest therein, whereas capital renovations made to a leased facility intended solely for use in an eligible SR&ED project throughout all or substantially all of their useful operating life constitute qualified SR&ED expenditures.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of the Blue Wave Seafoods decision reveals five interrelated legal, technical, and evidentiary failures that invalidated the vast majority of the Appellants' claims. These deficiencies illustrate the strict statutory separation in Canadian tax law between high-risk commercial market development and scientific or technological research.
2.1 Conflation of Commercial, Regulatory, and Resource Uncertainty with Technological Uncertainty

The foundational flaw in the Appellants' T661 filings was their macroscopic framing of the project as the "development of the silver hake fishery". In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence anchored by Northwest Hydraulic, the threshold requirement under subsection 248(1) of the Act is the existence of a scientific or technological uncertainty—a system-level or component-level limitation in scientific knowledge or engineering capability that cannot be resolved through standard practice, routine engineering, or existing industrial knowledge. The Appellants operated under the misconception that because the DFO designated the silver hake fishery as "developmental" or "exploratory," and because the Silver Hake Canadianization Committee had a mandate, as described in a Coopers & Lybrand Consulting study, to "Canadianize and commercialize" this underutilized species, all activities required to establish the domestic supply chain automatically qualified as SR&ED.

Justice Miller dismantled this premise by reducing the eight uncertainties listed in the Appellants' 1997 and 1998 technical description to the only three possible scientific or technological uncertainties he found facing the Appellants in those years. The first purported uncertainty was whether delicate silver hake could be stored onboard domestic fishing vessels as fresh fish without quality degradation. The Court found that the use of totes with a combination of ice and seawater resolved this problem, that the totes were being used at sea in 1997 and most likely before then, and that the use of totes was already known in the fishing industry in the early 1990s; it further noted that it was the fishers, not the Appellants, who were testing methods of handling the fish at sea, and that trying totes at someone's suggestion was routine or standard practice. The second purported uncertainty was whether sufficient biomass of silver hake existed in the inshore LaHave and Emerald basins to sustain a viable year-round domestic fishery. Justice Miller rejected the Respondent's position that this was merely a business uncertainty and held that the uncertainty was a scientific one; however, he found that the Appellants' efforts—sending Canadian fishers out at different times and collecting data—were standard or routine practice, and that the problem of fish population assessment was resolvable by standard or routine procedures, since scientists could make an estimate on which DFO would set the TAC, so that there was no scientific uncertainty facing the Appellants in this regard. The third purported uncertainty was whether fresh silver hake landed onshore could be processed and shipped as whole round fresh fish to commercial markets without loss of quality. By 1997 and 1998, the Appellants were effectively out of surimi and tempura production and were simply dumping fresh fish onto stainless steel tables, sorting for size and quality, weighing, icing, packaging, and shipping. Although the Court found that, given the delicacy of the fish and the fact that it had not been successfully marketed fresh to that point, there was a technological uncertainty in this respect, it held that nothing in the nature of testing any hypotheses was occurring and that the work was not characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment—it was processing fresh fish for sale.

The second-order insight emerging from this analysis is that economic risk, pioneering a new domestic market, or overcoming regulatory classifications does not create a technological uncertainty. Justice Miller explicitly rejected the Appellants' approach that if an activity is not "commercial" (for instance, because DFO may not have labelled the fishery commercial), it must be SR&ED, stating that for purposes of the Act it is not a test of default.
2.2 Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Scientific Method

Under the second and third prongs of the expanded Northwest Hydraulic framework, a taxpayer must demonstrate that it formulated specific hypotheses aimed at reducing an articulated technological uncertainty—proceeding through trained observation, clear objective setting, hypothesis articulation, and methodical testing—and executed procedures in accordance with established and objective principles of the scientific method.

While the Respondent acknowledged (so that the Court did not need to decide) that Blue Wave carried out SR&ED in 1995 and 1996 in developing surimi and tempura with machinery acquired from Japan, including a silent cutter and moulder—CRA's science advisor having recognized that processing silver hake was difficult due to the characteristics of the fish, their broader fishery claims and their 1997–1998 operations lacked any structured experimental protocol. In testimony, Mr. D'Eon acknowledged that the transition to 100-pound tote pans filled with slushy ice-water—the very mechanism that solved onboard freshness preservation—was implemented simply because "someone had simply suggested this to him". The Court held that simply trying totes already known in the fishing industry at an unidentified person's suggestion was routine or standard practice, and noted that it was the fishers rather than the Appellants who were testing handling methods at sea; adopting such a suggestion without formulating a scientific hypothesis, controlling variables (such as salinity ratios, thermal conductivity, compression depth, or enzymatic decay rates), or conducting systematic comparative analysis is the antithesis of the scientific method. Similarly, the onshore sorting and packaging of whole round silver hake in 1997 and 1998 involved zero systematic testing; it was standard commercial production.
2.3 Insufficient Contemporaneous Technical Documentation

The fifth criterion applied by Justice Miller requires that a detailed record be kept of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses. In Canadian SR&ED litigation, while oral testimony is admissible, a taxpayer bears the legal burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions through objective, contemporaneous documentary evidence demonstrating systematic investigation.

In Blue Wave Seafoods, the Court did not reach the fifth criterion, having disposed of 1997 and 1998 at the earlier stages of the analysis; the record nonetheless showed that CRA's science advisor noted in his 1996 report that no technical documentation was available for review, and the documentary evidence referred to in the judgment consisted largely of external government and consulting reports—such as the October 1992 DFO report on the 1991 silver hake processing experiments and the January 1995 Coopers & Lybrand funding proposal, both filed as Respondent's exhibits—alongside the production records, general ledgers, landing slips, and invoices reviewed by CRA's financial auditor. Because Mr. D'Eon believed the "science" of silver hake had been left primarily to industry (DFO lacking the funds to pursue all 21 underutilized species), the companies collected their own data from every boatload, including size, sex, weight, and length, but Mr. D'Eon was uncertain what analysis was done with this information, CRA's science advisor was concerned that nothing appeared to have been done with the data collected, and the Court found no evidence of any methodical or systematic testing of different methods of handling the fish onshore in 1997 and 1998. Furthermore, with respect to the $8,206 claimed for equipment (fire extinguishers, tables, and trays) in 1995, there was no testimony as to whether that amount pertained to the surimi and tempura production process, and the Court accordingly found that it did not qualify.
2.4 Statutory Misinterpretation of "Materials Consumed" and Commercial Procurement Commitments

One of the most consequential technical rulings in Blue Wave Seafoods concerns the treatment of bulk raw materials under the proxy method of SR&ED calculation. Having elected under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act, Blue Wave sought to claim the entire cost of fresh silver hake purchased from Canadian fishers at $0.15 per pound in 1995 and 1996. The Appellants advanced a two-fold legal argument: first, that all purchased fish constituted "materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V); and second—relying on Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen and inviting the Court to look to paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations for general interpretive guidance—that because they had no choice but to take the entire catch at $0.15 per pound (nearly double the $0.08 market price) to obtain the fresh fish needed for surimi development, and could neither dump it nor turn it into fish meal, the cost of the excess fish, sold only at a loss, was "directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED" under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations.

Justice Miller rejected both arguments by applying the ordinary meaning of the statutory language. Analyzing the ordinary grammatical and statutory meaning of "consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), the Court held that "consumed" means, in its ordinary and common-sense meaning (as applied by Associate Chief Justice Bowman in Consoltex), used up or rendered valueless—made waste—by the SR&ED process itself. Only the specific volume of silver hake that physically entered the experimental surimi and tempura dewatering, cutting, and moulding line was "consumed" in SR&ED. Because Blue Wave's leased plant lacked the processing capacity to convert the entire landed catch into surimi or tempura, the surplus fish was sold in a different form or frozen and placed into inventory (although some fish appear to have been sold as whole round fresh fish in the last couple of months of fiscal 1996). Justice Miller held that fish sold to customers or held in frozen inventory retained commercial monetary value and was not rendered waste by the SR&ED process.

Addressing paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations only as interpretive guidance (the Regulation not applying directly given the proxy election), the Court found that the fish would not have been bought at $0.15 per pound in 1995—and, as to the vast majority, in 1996—but for the surimi/tempura development, yet drew a sharp legal distinction between the cost of inputs used in experimentation and the cost of inventory sold in commercial operations. The outlays for excess fish were directly related to commercial product sales and inventory accumulation, not to the surimi SR&ED project. Crucially, the Court established that selling excess raw materials or non-SR&ED byproducts at a financial loss does not retroactively transform a commercial cost of goods sold into a qualified SR&ED expenditure.
2.5 Capital Expenditure Exclusions and the Leasehold Renovation Distinction

The final area of legal contention centred on the $27,914 claimed by Blue Wave in 1995 for third-party contractor outlays, which comprised $8,206 for plant equipment (fire extinguishers, tables, and trays) and $19,708 for renovations to the leased processing plant to accommodate surimi production. Regarding the $8,206 equipment outlay, the failure was evidentiary: there was no testimony as to whether these general plant safety and fish-handling items pertained to the surimi/tempura production process, so the Court found the amount did not qualify without needing to reach the "all or substantially all" (90% or greater) SR&ED usage threshold required for capital equipment prior to the 2014 repeal of capital SR&ED eligibility.

Conversely, on the $19,708 renovation expenditure, it was the CRA that committed an error of law. The Minister had disallowed the $19,708 pursuant to subparagraph 37(8)(d)(i) of the Act, taking the position that renovations to a leased plant constituted an excluded capital expenditure on a "leasehold interest in a building". Justice Miller overturned the Minister on this point, holding that subparagraph 37(8)(d)(i) only precludes capital expenditures made for the acquisition of a building or the acquisition of a leasehold interest in a building. Capital expenditures incurred to renovate an already-leased facility—where the evidence establishes that the renovations were intended to be used solely in connection with the prosecution of an eligible SR&ED project during all or substantially all of their useful operating life—are not barred by subparagraph 37(8)(d)(i) and therefore qualified as eligible SR&ED expenditures in 1995.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement adjudicated in Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. The Queen against the specific deficiencies in the Appellants' claims and the evidentiary standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: The Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof

cells: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1)

Claimed the macro-project of "developing a Canadian inshore silver hake fishery" in 1997–1998. Relied on DFO's "exploratory/developmental" regulatory designation and listed eight uncertainties (gear, deployment, handling, economic return, by-catch, cost targets, larger fish, mesh openings), which the Court reduced to three possible uncertainties: onboard storage, stock abundance in the LaHave/Emerald basins, and onshore handling.

The taxpayer must prove an objective limitation in scientific knowledge or technological capability that cannot be resolved by standard practice or routine engineering. Stock abundance was held to be a scientific (not merely business) uncertainty, but one resolvable by standard or routine procedures (scientific estimates on which DFO sets the TAC); onboard storage had already been resolved by totes; only onshore handling presented a technological uncertainty, which failed on the hypothesis and scientific-method criteria.
Disallowed (1997–1998): Appeals for both Blue Wave and D'Eon dismissed; zero SR&ED found in 1997 and 1998.
Formulation of Hypotheses & Scientific Method (Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criteria 2 & 3)

Claimed onboard fresh fish preservation (using 100-lb slush-ice totes) and onshore whole-round fresh fish handling (dumping on stainless steel tables, sorting, icing, packing) as experimental development. Slush-ice totes were used at sea by the fishers (not the Appellants) simply because "someone had simply suggested this" without systematic testing.

The taxpayer must demonstrate trained observation, clear objective setting, formal articulation of a hypothesis, and methodical, systematic testing governed by objective scientific principles. Adopting known industry techniques or informal suggestions is routine engineering/operations.
Disallowed (1997–1998): Onboard tote usage and onshore whole-round sorting/packing held to be known, routine commercial processes.
Technological Advancement (Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4)

Asserted that proving silver hake could be harvested fresh by domestic inshore vessels and sold whole-round in commercial markets constituted a technological advancement for the Canadian fishing industry.

The process must generate new scientific knowledge or advance underlying technology beyond the existing state of the art. The Court did not reach this criterion: the 1995–1996 surimi/tempura work was acknowledged as eligible by the Respondent (CRA's science advisor having found a technological advancement in developing a process for a fish with such different characteristics), and the 1997–1998 claims failed at the earlier criteria.

Allowed in Part (1995–1996 Surimi only); Disallowed (1997–1998): Only the 1995–1996 surimi/tempura processing sub-project was accepted as eligible, by the Respondent's acknowledgment rather than a judicial finding on technological advancement.
Contemporaneous Detailed Record-Keeping (Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5)

CRA's science advisor noted that no technical documentation was available for his 1996 review; the Appellants collected size, sex, weight, and length data, but nothing appeared to have been done with it. Adduced no testimony as to whether $8,206 of 1995 equipment pertained to surimi R&D.

Detailed, contemporaneous records must be maintained of each hypothesis, experimental test protocol, and quantitative/qualitative result as the work progresses, alongside specific evidence linking claimed outlays to the eligible SR&ED project.

Disallowed: The Court did not reach the record-keeping criterion for 1997–1998 (the claims failed at earlier criteria); the $8,206 in 1995 equipment costs was disallowed for lack of testimony linking it to the surimi/tempura process.
Materials Consumed in the Prosecution of SR&ED (Act s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V))

Under the proxy method election, claimed 100% of third-party fresh silver hake purchased at $0.15/lb in 1995–1996, including excess catch beyond surimi plant capacity that was frozen in inventory or sold commercially as whole/non-surimi fish.

To be "consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED," materials must physically pass through the experimental process and be used up or rendered valueless (made waste) by it. Excess materials sold commercially or held in inventory retain value and are not "consumed".
Disallowed (1995–1996): All fish costs beyond the exact quantities processed into surimi/tempura as allowed by CRA were rejected.
Expenditures Directly Related to SR&ED (Regulation 2900(2)(c); Act s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II))

Argued that offering $0.15/lb (above the $0.08/lb market rate) for the entire catch was required to secure fresh fish for surimi R&D, making the cost of the excess fish (sold only at a loss) an expenditure directly related to SR&ED.

Regulation 2900(2)(c) did not apply directly given the proxy election and was considered only as interpretive guidance; under it, an expenditure must be directly related to the experimental prosecution itself and be one that would not have been incurred but for it. Costs of excess raw materials sold commercially relate directly to product sales/inventory; selling non-SR&ED inventory at a loss does not convert a commercial cost into an SR&ED outlay.
Disallowed (1995–1996): Commercial losses on excess fish purchases held not to be directly related to SR&ED prosecution.
Capital Expenditures on Leased Buildings vs. Renovations (Act s. 37(8)(d)(i), s. 38)

Claimed $19,708 in 1995 contractor costs for renovating the leased plant to accommodate surimi machinery. CRA disallowed the outlay under s. 37(8)(d)(i) as an excluded capital expenditure on a leasehold interest in a building.

Under pre-2014 capital rules, s. 37(8)(d)(i) precludes only the capital cost of acquiring a leasehold interest in a building, not capital renovations to a leased building intended to be used solely for SR&ED throughout all or substantially all of their useful operating life.
Allowed (1995): Blue Wave's 1995 appeal allowed in part; $19,708 in surimi plant renovations held to be a qualified SR&ED expenditure.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. The Queen into actionable tax and engineering compliance protocols for contemporary Canadian claimants, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic corporate scenarios confronting the exact statutory pitfalls identified by Justice Miller. While Justice Miller allowed capital plant renovations in 1995 based on pre-2014 statutory rules, subsequent legislative amendments to paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act repealed capital expenditures and leasehold improvements from SR&ED qualification for outlays incurred after December 31, 2013 (capital expenditure eligibility was subsequently reinstated by Bill C-15, the Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, for property acquired, or lease costs incurred, after December 15, 2024). Consequently, for outlays made between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024—and as a conservative practice thereafter—remedial structuring must address facility modifications through current-account prototype integration, ephemeral pilot plant teardowns, or eligible subcontractor service structures alongside strict material consumption tracking.
Case Study 1: Marine Bio-Processing & Novel Protein Extraction (Atlantic Pelagic Valorization Inc.)
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

Atlantic Pelagic Valorization Inc. ("APV"), a Nova Scotia agri-food and marine biotechnology processor, initiates a multi-year initiative to commercialize Atlantic argentine (Argentina silus), an underutilized, high-lipid, fragile mesopelagic fish species historically avoided by domestic fleets. APV files an umbrella Form T661 claim titled "Development of a Domestic Atlantic Argentine Bio-Extraction Fishery." In structuring this claim, APV encounters three severe audit vulnerabilities directly mirroring the failures in Blue Wave Seafoods. First, APV conflates macro-level supply chain development with technological research by claiming offshore acoustic biomass mapping to determine seasonal catch stability, the installation of standard refrigerated seawater (RSW) chilling tanks on contracted trawlers based on a marine equipment vendor's informal recommendation, and onshore automated grading and blast-freezing of whole argentine. Second, APV buries its genuine core technical project within these commercial operations: inside its leased plant, APV is conducting experimental enzymatic hydrolysis to extract low-molecular-weight bioactive collagen peptides from argentine skin and bones, where high endogenous cathepsin enzymes and lipid oxidation cause severe emulsion breakdown and bitter off-flavours during membrane ultrafiltration. Third, electing the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), APV offers inshore fishers a guaranteed floor price of $0.40/lb (double the $0.20/lb bait-market rate) with a mandatory "take-all-catch" covenant to secure ultra-fresh argentine. APV lands 500,000 lbs of fish ($200,000 total cost), but its pilot enzymatic bioreactors only have the capacity to process 40,000 lbs. The remaining 460,000 lbs are blast-frozen and sold into the commercial pet-food and bait markets at a net loss of $0.22/lb. APV claims the full $200,000 fish cost as "materials consumed" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) and claims $45,000 in lump-sum contractor invoices covering general plant drainage upgrades, stainless steel sorting tables, and custom sacrificial bioreactor piping.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Technical Boundary Delineation

To prevent the CRA Science Advisor from disqualifying the entire claim as commercial fishery development—as occurred in Blue Wave Seafoods for the 1997 and 1998 taxation years—APV must immediately abandon the macroscopic T661 project definition and establish a formal SR&ED Steering Committee comprising the Lead Bioprocess Engineer, the Plant Operations Manager, and external Canadian tax counsel. Through this governance body, APV must formally excise offshore biomass mapping (stock-assessment work that, per Justice Miller's ruling, may raise a scientific uncertainty but one resolvable by standard or routine procedures), onboard RSW chilling tank usage (the adoption of known industry techniques without systematic hypothesis testing), and onshore whole-fish grading and blast-freezing (routine commercial processing) from the SR&ED claim boundary. Instead, the T661 project scope must be strictly ring-fenced around the specific biochemical and process engineering uncertainties: overcoming lipid-induced membrane fouling and endogenous cathepsin proteolysis during dual-stage enzymatic hydrolysis and tangential-flow ultrafiltration of high-lipid mesopelagic fish substrates. Project governance charters must mandate that internal SR&ED project cost-centres are activated only when raw fish substrates cross the physical threshold of the pilot hydrolysis reactor bay.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Record-Keeping

To satisfy the five-part Northwest Hydraulic test applied by Justice Miller, APV must replace general commercial catch logs and third-party market feasibility studies with a contemporaneous, five-stage experimental documentation protocol maintained in an immutable electronic laboratory notebook (ELN). The engineering team must first document specific baseline failures demonstrating why standard salmon or cod hydrolysis protocols fail when applied to Atlantic argentine, such as recording a baseline permeate flux decline of 68% within 45 minutes on 10 kDa polyethersulfone membranes due to phospholipid micelle binding. Next, the team must explicitly articulate the technological uncertainty as a system-level conflict between the thermal deactivation of endogenous cathepsins (requiring temperatures above 75 °C, which accelerates polyunsaturated fatty acid oxidation) and the preservation of native peptide bioactivity during alcalase and flavourzyme digestion. Governance rules must require every pilot batch run to be preceded by a logged, falsifiable hypothesis—for example, testing whether implementing a sub-critical two-stage isoelectric pre-wash at pH 4.8 with a 0.15% citric acid chelator at 4 °C prior to 52 °C alcalase hydrolysis will reduce unbound neutral lipids by over 80% and maintain tangential-flow ultrafiltration permeate flux above 35 L/m²h without denaturing Type I collagen chains. Finally, technicians must log controlled variable adjustments (enzyme-to-substrate ratios, shear rates, transmembrane pressures, degree of hydrolysis [%DH] curves, and peroxide values) alongside post-run analytical chemistry data (such as HPLC molecular weight distribution profiles) confirming or refuting each hypothesis as the work progresses.
Step 3: Contractual Terms and Supply/Contractor Structuring

APV must restructure both its raw fish procurement agreements and its third-party engineering contractor agreements to eliminate the commingling of commercial and experimental outlays that proved fatal in Blue Wave Seafoods. Rather than executing a single undifferentiated "take-all-catch" commercial supply agreement at $0.40/lb, APV must execute a Master Supply Agreement containing two legally and operationally distinct schedules. Schedule A (Dedicated R&D Pilot Substrate Supply) must contract specifically for small-lot, precision-handled experimental batches (up to 40,000 lbs) harvested under specific time-temperature logging protocols and delivered directly to the Pilot Hydrolysis Bay in segregated, barcoded insulated totes, with the $0.40/lb price contractually designated as a technical handling fee for R&D substrate specification compliance. Schedule B (Commercial Bulk Catch Off-Take) must govern all commercial volume beyond Schedule A (460,000 lbs); even if APV pays a commercial price premium or subsidizes fishers to secure fleet loyalty, Schedule B costs must be booked exclusively to Commercial Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and excluded from the SR&ED claim, respecting Justice Miller's holding that commercial losses on excess catch cannot be claimed as SR&ED. Similarly, for the $45,000 contractor spend, APV must require vendors to issue separate Statements of Work (SOWs) and itemized invoices distinguishing routine plant equipment—such as stainless steel sorting tables and safety gear, which failed in Blue Wave Seafoods for lack of evidentiary nexus—from eligible current SR&ED engineering services, such as the custom fabrication and destructive testing of non-reusable sacrificial titanium-alloy ultrasonic cavitation nozzles integrated directly into the pilot bioreactor loop under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Cost Allocation

To survive a CRA Financial Audit under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act (paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations being, per Blue Wave Seafoods, inapplicable to a taxpayer that has made the proxy election and relevant at most as interpretive guidance), APV must implement a strict mass-balance material tracking ledger at the pilot plant floor level. Under this protocol, only the exact weight of Atlantic argentine physically loaded into the pilot hydrolysis reactors (40,000 lbs at $0.40/lb = $16,000), plus the specific industrial enzymes, food-grade acids, buffers, and fouled single-use ultrafiltration membranes destroyed during pilot trials, are recorded under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V). To satisfy Justice Miller's strict definition of "consumed"—meaning used up or rendered valueless (made waste) by the SR&ED process—every experimental batch of collagen peptide hydrolysate must be tracked through to destructive analytical testing and certified waste disposal. APV must maintain signed Waste Destruction Certificates and municipal bio-waste disposal manifests proving that the resulting 40,000 lbs of digested protein slurry and spent bone cake were neither sold as commercial bait or pet food nor placed into commercial inventory. If any experimental peptide batch is subsequently sold as a commercial sample or used in commercial feed formulations, that specific batch must be reclassified from "materials consumed" to "materials transformed" and subjected to the SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the Act, or excluded upfront if the output was never rendered valueless.
Case Study 2: Hydrometallurgical Critical Mineral Extraction & Pilot Plant Scaling (Northern Shield Lithium Corp.)
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

Northern Shield Lithium Corp. ("NSLC"), an Alberta and Ontario-based mineral processing enterprise, seeks to extract battery-grade lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃) from unconventional, low-grade Devonian oilfield brines heavily contaminated with magnesium, calcium, hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), and suspended petroleum hydrocarbons. NSLC submits an overarching SR&ED claim titled "Development of a Commercial Canadian Oilfield Brine Lithium Industry," exhibiting four classic defects adjudicated in Blue Wave Seafoods. First, NSLC claims 18 months of hydrogeological well-flow testing and reservoir brine sampling across twelve depleted oilfield leases to determine whether lithium concentrations (averaging 65 mg/L) and aquifer recharge rates are sufficient to support a 20,000-tonne-per-year commercial plant—paralleling the Appellants' disallowed effort in Blue Wave Seafoods to determine whether silver hake biomass in the LaHave and Emerald basins could sustain a year-round fishery. Second, while NSLC conducts genuine chemical engineering SR&ED in Years 1 and 2 to synthesize a novel titanium-intercalated manganese oxide (HTO) Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE) adsorbent bead resistant to H₂S reductive dissolution, it continues in Years 3 and 4 to claim the ongoing operation of a skid-mounted field unit where operators simply pump raw brine through commercial bag filters and standard activated carbon columns (adopted after a water-treatment vendor suggested it) and ship concentrated lithium chloride (LiCl) eluate to a toll processor. Third, under a joint-venture brine access agreement, NSLC pays an oilfield operator a flat fee of $15.00 per cubic metre for a minimum mandatory draw of 100,000 m³ of raw brine ($1,500,000), plus $300,000 in bulk industrial hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃). NSLC's pilot DLE column only processes 8,000 m³ of brine; the remaining 92,000 m³ of brine and bulk reagents are used to produce industrial calcium-magnesium road de-icing brine, which NSLC sells to municipalities at a steep financial loss to dispose of the volume, claiming the full $1,800,000 as "materials consumed" in SR&ED. Fourth, NSLC claims $120,000 in contractor invoices for modifying a leased industrial warehouse in Edmonton, mixing structural ventilation and epoxy floor upgrades for the DLE acid-stripping pilot rig with standard warehouse forklifts, eyewash stations, fire extinguishers, and steel storage racks.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Technical Boundary Delineation

NSLC must restructure its internal R&D governance to enforce a hard statutory separation between mineral resource exploration (governed by the Canadian Exploration Expense [CEE] regime under section 66.1 of the Act, where applicable, or standard business operating expenses) and chemical process SR&ED under section 37 and subsection 248(1). All hydrogeological reservoir testing, aquifer flow-rate monitoring, and brine reserve estimations must be stripped from the T661 claim; just as Justice Miller held that silver hake abundance in the Nova Scotia basins, although a scientific uncertainty, was resolvable by standard or routine procedures and did not render the Appellants' activities SR&ED, oilfield brine reservoir capacity and grade consistency assessments should be excluded as resource evaluation work (exploring for minerals being expressly excluded under paragraph (h) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1)). Furthermore, NSLC's governance protocols must institute an annual "Technical Gate Review" at the end of each fiscal year. Once the HTO adsorbent bead synthesis and H₂S passivation chemistry achieve stable cycle performance at the conclusion of Year 2, that sub-project must be formally closed unless a new, distinct technological uncertainty arises during scale-up, such as hydrodynamic channelling and bead attrition under high-pressure counter-current fluidized bed operation. The routine Year 3 and Year 4 operation of vendor-suggested bag filters and activated carbon columns must be classified as standard commercial pre-treatment, preventing a total audit rejection akin to Blue Wave Seafoods' 1997 and 1998 claims.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Record-Keeping

To substantiate that any Year 3 and Year 4 pilot work constitutes genuine experimental development rather than routine brine processing, NSLC must implement a strict scientific documentation architecture mapped directly to the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria applied in Blue Wave Seafoods. Whenever NSLC engineers test pre-treatment or DLE column scaling parameters, project governance must prohibit informal trial-and-error vendor suggestions. Instead, every modification must be initiated via a formal Engineering Change & Hypothesis Record (ECHR) specifying the exact mass-transfer or thermodynamic uncertainty—for example, quantifying the competitive ion-exchange kinetics between divalent Mg²⁺ at concentrations exceeding 12,000 mg/L and monovalent Li⁺ at 65 mg/L within a 3-metre pulsed-bed HTO column under fluctuating thermal profiles. NSLC must pair these ECHRs with contemporaneous analytical logs by maintaining automated SCADA data-historian records linked directly to ICP-OES (Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy) assay sheets for every feed, raffinate, and eluate cycle, alongside X-ray diffraction (XRD) crystal lattice degradation analyses of spent HTO adsorbent beads. This creates an unassailable contemporaneous record of hypothesis, test, and result as the work progresses.
Step 3: Contractual Terms and Supply/Contractor Structuring

NSLC must overhaul its commercial brine supply contracts and engineering vendor agreements to establish an unmistakable nexus to SR&ED prosecution (recognizing that, under Blue Wave Seafoods, paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations does not apply directly to a taxpayer that has made the proxy election and serves at most as interpretive guidance). To eliminate take-or-pay commingling in brine supply, NSLC must renegotiate its joint-venture brine access agreement to separate commercial disposal and road-salt operations from R&D feedstock procurement. The contract must establish a dedicated R&D Slipstream Metering Clause whereby NSLC pays a metered unit price strictly for the 8,000 m³ of sour brine diverted through a calibrated flow-meter into the experimental DLE pilot loop, with spent raffinate returned directly to the operator's deep-well injection disposal line. If NSLC commercially elects to process the remaining 92,000 m³ into municipal road de-icer, those brine and reagent costs must be contractually isolated in a separate commercial operating account; under Blue Wave Seafoods, selling road de-icer at a financial loss cannot convert those 92,000 m³ of brine into an SR&ED expense. Simultaneously, to avoid the disallowance suffered by Blue Wave on its $8,206 equipment claim, NSLC must instruct contractors to separate general facility safety and material-handling equipment (forklifts, eyewash stations, fire extinguishers, and storage racks) onto standard commercial capital or expense invoices. For custom pilot-plant engineering work, NSLC must structure contracts as current-account Custom Prototype Fabrication and Destructive Testing Services under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act, explicitly specifying in the contract that custom-fabricated PVDF acid-stripping columns and sacrificial sensor arrays are non-commercial, single-purpose experimental apparatuses that will be dismantled and scrapped upon completion of the hypothesis testing program.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Cost Allocation

To ensure full compliance with subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act under the proxy method, NSLC must institute an ERP-integrated SR&ED Material Consumption Ledger. NSLC must install calibrated inline mass-flow meters on the DLE pilot skid inputs for raw brine, HCl eluent, and Na₂CO₃ precipitation reagents so that only the exact stoichiometric and flushing volumes metered into the experimental DLE skid (8,000 m³ of brine costing $120,000, plus the exact mass of HCl, Na₂CO₃, and degraded HTO adsorbent resin beads physically destroyed or chemically exhausted during column cycling) are coded to the SR&ED "Materials Consumed" general ledger account. Because Justice Miller held in Blue Wave Seafoods that materials retaining monetary value in inventory or commercial sales are not "consumed", any off-spec lithium carbonate filter cake precipitated during pilot runs must be physically quarantined from commercial inventory. Portion samples consumed in destructive purity assays (such as ICP-OES, scanning electron microscopy, and coin-cell battery electrochemical cycling tests) or neutralized and disposed of as hazardous chemical waste are fully eligible as "materials consumed". Conversely, if any pilot-scale LiCl eluate or Li₂CO₃ powder is shipped to a toll processor for commercial sale or held in commercial product inventory, its corresponding raw material input cost must be carved out of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) or subjected to SR&ED ITC recapture.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled the processing adjustments were routine commercial development without technological uncertainty.
